Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:1: This chapter shall explain the passage we quoted above, "Do not defile yourselves through them, lest you become impure (unetmetem) through them" (Leviticus 11:43): "if a person defiles himself a little," and so on (Yoma 39a). It would have been fitting to explain this passage first, since that is its order in the Gemara passage, but we were compelled by the connection of the discourse we were engaged in regarding holiness — for it is all one matter, and this passage too is largely explained by what was explained above in the three divisions, "a great deal," "from above," "in/for the World to Come" — for the same pattern applies also regarding impurity. Nevertheless, we saw fit to explain in it something further, for there is no exposition without some new insight, and it too pertains to our discourse — for by a person's knowing how to separate from impurity, he will become holy through it. And so our holy Torah, in Parashat Shemini, after mentioning the impurity of foods, says, "and you shall sanctify yourselves" (Leviticus 11:44), and likewise in Parashat Kedoshim regarding forbidden relations.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:2: Although it would seem that the opposite of impurity is purity, as explained above regarding the word "purity," the Torah has explained to us that holiness, too, is the opposite of impurity. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained the reason for this in the Mechilta, on the verse "and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6), saying, in these words: "a holy nation" — He called them a holy nation, as it is said, "and who is like Your people Israel, a unique (echad) nation" (II Samuel 7:23); and "a holy nation" — holy and sanctified, separated from the nations of the world — so far his words. Thus he explained the word "holiness" to mean separation from the nations of the world, which is impurity. Since this is so, we saw fit to explain everything found in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that speaks of separation from impurity, insofar as it pertains to this passage, so that a person may become holy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:3: It says, "if a person defiles himself a little, they defile him a great deal" — according to the manner explained above, it is clear that it means: a person defiles himself with one transgression, and they defile him a great deal, for one transgression draws another.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:4: It might also be said that "they defile him a great deal" is in the manner of what they said (Shabbat 104a), "whoever comes to defile himself, they open the way for him" — meaning he has many openings through which he may become defiled. And in this same manner it says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach 169b): whoever comes to be defiled, that impure spirit draws itself upon him and attaches itself to him, and there are many [spirits] ready to defile him, and they defile him, and he becomes impure, and they defile him in this world and in that world — so far his words. It says, "there are many [spirits] ready..." and so on, and the reason, as explained in Parashat Vayechi (228a), is that the kelipot are called "Lo-Ammi" ("not My people"), ready to rest upon a person for nothing — this is "they defile him a great deal," for each one wishes to gain possession of him and says, "He is mine."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:5: One might also explain the phrase "a person defiles himself a little" to mean that there are impurities not mentioned in the Torah, which is a tradition of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that a person defiles himself through them. In the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, end, 53b — approximately) Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains that one who sleeps at night has the spirit of impurity resting upon his hands, and upon waking it is not fitting for him to touch his garments or anywhere else until he washes his hands. In these words: Come and see, all the people of the world, at the hour they sleep in their beds at night, and the night spreads its wings over all the people of the world, taste the taste of death; and because they taste the taste of death, that impure spirit rests upon the world and defiles the world within its embrace, and it rests upon their hands and they become defiled; and when he wakes and his soul returns to him, whatever he touches with his hands is all defiled, because an impure spirit rests upon them. Therefore a person should not take garments to wear from one who has not washed his hands, for that impure spirit has been drawn upon him and he has become defiled, and that impure spirit has license to rest wherever it finds a mark of its own side. Therefore a person should not wash his hands [with water] from one who has not washed his own hands, because that impure spirit is drawn upon him and clings to whoever takes water from him, and it has license to rest upon that person. Therefore a person must guard himself on all his sides from the side of this evil serpent, lest it rule over him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:6: In this same manner is what is explained elsewhere: that upon waking from sleep, one should not walk four cubits before washing [his hands]; and if he walks four cubits with the spirit of impurity still on his hands, he is like one who worships idols. Concerning this it is said, "of him who is brought by the hand of God" (Job 12:6, according to this reading).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:7: Similar to these, which will be explained, are minor impurities that a person tramples with his heels; and if he defiles himself with these, they will defile him a great deal, with impurities like them, and from these he will come to severe impurities.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:8: And in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz 198b) it counted the matter of washing the hands in the morning among the sins that a person tramples with his heels, on the verse, "Why should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me" (Psalms 49:6), and it explains there that the kelipah has days that are called "days of evil," and concerning this David said, "Why should I fear in the days of evil, when the iniquity of my heels surrounds me" — in these words: what are these "days of evil"? These are the days that are appointed for that evil one — and who is this? This is the evil inclination, which is called "evil," and it has known days on which it is given license in the world to defile all those who defile their ways — for whoever comes to be defiled, they defile him — and these are called "days of evil," and they are appointed over those sins that people trample with their heels. Come and see, all who defile their ways — how many bands of destroyers are appointed for them, defiling them; on the very path that a person wishes to walk, on that path they literally lead him astray. When a person comes to purify himself, how many [angels] assist him! Behold, we have learned that when a person arises in the morning he must wash his hands from a basin of water, which is a vessel from which to take water, from one who has already washed his hands beforehand, as they have established. Come and see, for the sake of this we have established the matter of the basin; and further, that a person should wash his right hand [together] with his left, in order for the right to rule over the left, and the right is washed [with water poured] from the left — and for this reason it is called "washing." And therefore, whoever washes his hands should wash the right with the left, to give the right dominion over the left, so as not to give the evil inclination any place to rule at all — and this has already been established — so far his words. Behold, all these are precise details of the commandment that assist a person in becoming pure, and if he tramples them with his heels, they defile him, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:9: Similarly, they said in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot 77a), in these words: these matters King Solomon revealed in the book of Ashmedai the king, and I found in it one thousand four hundred and fifty kinds of impurity by which people become defiled, which Ashmedai revealed to King Solomon — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:10: Among the impurities, one must be careful of what they said in the Gemara (Horayot 13b): passing between two women, between two camels, and all those things that cause forgetting of one's learning — which we shall quote below, please God — all of these are minor impurities not mentioned in the Torah, which a person tramples with his heels. Included in this is what they said in the Gemara (Makkot 16b), that one who holds back his bodily needs transgresses "do not make your souls detestable" (Leviticus 11:43), and likewise one who drinks from the horn used by a bloodletter — these are minor impurities that a person tramples with his heels. And likewise several things that the commentators, of blessed memory, explained require washing the hands: such as one who cuts his fingernails, one who removes his shoes, one who touches his feet, one who washes his head, and many similar things that Rabbi Yosef Karo, may his light shine, quoted in Beit Yosef (Tur Orach Chaim, siman 4).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:11: "From below," "they defile him from above" — already explained regarding holiness, and in that same manner they defile him above: when his soul ascends above every night, they distance themselves from him and proclaim of him that he is impure.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:12: Further, as we quoted in the Gate of Awe, chapter 9, that several angels curse him and say, "Remove yourselves from around so-and-so, for there is testimony against him, and an impure spirit rests upon him" (Parashat Acharei, 76a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:13: But there are further aspects of this found in the words of Rashbi that are fitting to quote here. "From below" may be explained to mean that a person defiles himself with the powers of Na'amah that spread out below among people, appearing to them in the guise of beautiful women, causing them to emit seed in vain, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit 55a) — see there — in these words: Rabbi Shimon said, woe to those people who do not know, do not take heed, and do not consider, and are all sealed up, not knowing how full the world is with strange creatures unseen and with hidden matters — for if permission were given to the eye to see, people would be amazed how they could survive in the world. Come and see, this Na'amah, the mother of demons, was, and so on — see there. And the word "below" fits better with this interpretation than with what was explained before, because these powers are below the firmament, and the whole air is filled with them, as explained, and further, they spread out below among human beings.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:14: Rashbi explains there, just before this, that these powers attach themselves only to one who is of their own kind, in these words: Come and see, any person who goes toward the left side and defiles his ways draws all impure spirits upon himself, and an impure spirit attaches itself to him and does not leave him; and that impure spirit's attachment is to this person and not to another, and therefore their attachment is only to those who attach themselves to them. Fortunate are the righteous who walk in a straight path, who are truly righteous, and their children are fortunate in the world, and of them it is written, "for the upright shall dwell in the land" (Proverbs 2:21) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:15: And so it says likewise in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach 169b) that when a person walks in a straight path, these powers do not encounter him, and of him it is said, "No evil shall befall you" (Psalms 91:10), which is Lilith, "nor shall any plague come near your tent" — and plagues (nega) refer to the afflictions of human beings.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:16: "They defile him from above" may be explained by what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Metzora 54a), in these words: what is [meant by] "all the days of the flow of her impurity" (Leviticus 15:25)? Rather, the wicked defile themselves through their sins. In this same manner, in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit 54a), it says that if a person sins and the spirit of impurity rests upon him, and he fathers a son before he returns in repentance, that son is drawn after him with the power of impurity, in these words: Come and see, at the hour a person walks in a true path and draws upon himself a supernal holy spirit and attaches himself to it, the son that he fathers into the world draws upon himself supernal holiness, and he will be holy with the holiness of his Master, as it is written, "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy..." (Leviticus 20:7). And when he walks on the left side and draws an impure spirit upon himself and attaches himself to it, the son that comes forth from him into the world draws an impure spirit upon himself and becomes defiled with the impurity of that side; and concerning this it is written, "Who knows the spirit of the sons of man, whether it goes upward..." (Ecclesiastes 3:21) — so far his words, as pertains to our subject. And my teacher, peace be upon him, testified concerning a certain Jewish young man who converted to the religion of the Ishmaelites, and afterward converted to yet another religion, and it was testified concerning him that these two transgressions were [committed] by his father.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:17: Let us return to our subject: in this same manner one might explain "they sanctify him from above" — that he draws down a holy soul for his son, and this is included in everything explained above regarding "they sanctify him from above."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:18: Now, according to the manner explained above regarding "he sanctifies himself below," which is the holiness of the five senses, we would need to elaborate here at length on the impurity of the senses — if he defiles them, how great is the blemish and impurity that comes upon him; but since we shall need below to explain the holiness of the five senses, each on its own, we shall likewise explain the matter of their impurity in passing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:19: "In this world, they defile him for the World to Come" — according to the manner explained above regarding "this world," which is the holiness of thought, so too regarding impurity, it is the defilement of thought in all matters of this world, and its punishment is severe: they defile him for the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:20: The reason is that the limbs act only in partnership with thought — whether toward holiness or the reverse — and regarding holiness we have already explained; regarding impurity, there are aspects to it, for one who sins by chance is not comparable to one who plots schemes for how to commit the transgression. For just as, in holiness, a good thought for a mitzvah effects a rectification above, so an evil thought of transgression causes a blemish in the world of thought, though it is exempted from there [from full punishment] — meaning that only when his thought is carried out in deed is he judged even for the thought. By this, the verses and passages of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, can be reconciled — for they said (Kiddushin 40a), "an evil thought — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join it to the deed," as it is said, "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard" (Psalms 66:18); yet we find that King David, peace be upon him, said elsewhere, "He plots iniquity upon his bed, he sets himself in a way that is not good..." (Psalms 36:5) — showing that the evil thought is indeed reckoned, but on the condition we explained — when the evil thought is carried into deed, that is, "he sets himself in a way that is not good."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:21: And so they said in the Midrash (Yalkut Isaiah, remez 395) on the verse, "Say of the righteous, that it shall be well [with him]..." (Isaiah 3:10), in these words: a good thought — the Holy One, blessed be He, joins it to the deed, as it is said, "then those who feared the Lord spoke to one another..." (Malachi 3:16) — what is [meant by] "and to those who thought upon His name"? Rabbi Yosei said, even if he thought to perform a mitzvah and did not perform it, the verse accounts it to him as though he had performed it. An evil thought — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join it to the deed, as it is said, "If I had regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard" (Psalms 66:18). But then what is [meant by], "Behold, I bring upon this people the fruit of their thoughts" (cf. Jeremiah 6:19)? A thought that produces fruit — the Holy One, blessed be He, joins it to the deed; one that does not produce fruit — the Holy One, blessed be He, does not join it to the deed. "And I will ensnare the house of Israel by their own heart" (Ezekiel 14:5) — this is written regarding idolatry — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:22: In the manner we have explained, one might call "a thought that produces fruit" one that is either carried out in deed or not carried out — for example, he thought to steal and did steal, or did not steal.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:23: One might also say "a thought that produces fruit" refers to what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avodah Zarah 20b), "and you shall guard yourself from every evil thing" (Deuteronomy 23:10) — that one should not fantasize by day and come to impurity at night; behold, this is the thought from which an evil fruit emerges — namely, the impurity of a seminal emission, which gives birth to a demon or a harmful spirit in the world, for the children a person fathers are called his "fruit," as is known. But when the thought does not come to impurity, it is a thought that produces no fruit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:24: That is, when he lingers greatly in that fantasy and brings himself to dwell upon it, as they said in tractate Niddah (13b), "whoever brings himself to dwell upon [lustful] fantasy is not admitted within the precincts of the Holy One, blessed be He," as it is said, "evil shall not sojourn with You" (Psalms 5:5) — for then he certainly comes to impurity and emits seed in vain, which is called "evil," as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Shelach 158a). But if a fantasy comes to him and he pushes it from his heart, then he has produced no fruit, and it is not accounted to him as the sin of dwelling on fantasy — for they said, of blessed memory (Bava Batra 164b), that there are three things from which a person is not saved every day, and one of them is thoughts of transgression. And concerning such a fantasy that does produce fruit is what is said in this passage — that if he defiles himself in this world, they defile him for the World to Come. And how is this precisely fitting with the word "this world"? Because this world became corrupted through the sin of Adam, "and they knew that they were naked" (Genesis 3:7), and they became aware of the matter of nakedness (ervah), which was not so before. It follows that if he sanctifies his thought so as not to think of women, they sanctify him; and likewise in the reverse, as stated.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:25: And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Kedoshim 24:6), that all holiness is holiness from forbidden relations, in these words: Why is the portion of forbidden relations juxtaposed to the portion of Kedoshim? To teach you that wherever you find a fence against forbidden relations, you find holiness, and whoever guards himself from forbidden relations is called holy. Rabbi Yehoshua of Sichnin, in the name of Rabbi Levi, brings this from the Shunammite woman, this being what is written, "and she said to her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is a holy man of God" (II Kings 4:9) — he is holy, and his attendant [Gehazi] is not holy — this teaches that [Elisha] never looked upon her. The Rabbis say she never saw [him unclothed], and so on. The maidservant of Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, I used to attend to the garments of my master, and I never in all my days saw anything improper upon my master's garments — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:26: Now, since we find all these aspects regarding a woman's nakedness (ervah), which is called "holiness," so too the holiness of thought is called simply "holiness," which encompasses everything — for even if a person sees a woman, if he does not let his heart's thought dwell upon her, the sight does not harm him. And the proof of this is that Rabbi Yehudah bar Ila'i would dance with the bride and it was to him as a beam of wood (cf. Ketubot 17a), and likewise a certain rabbi to whom [women] appeared as white geese (Berachot 20a) — all of this because their thoughts were separated from the affairs of this world and always attached to the Name, blessed be He.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:27: And so, if he defiles his thought with matters of forbidden relations, he certainly defiles himself for the World to Come, being uprooted from there, as is elaborated in the Zohar, in the Tosefta (Parashat Vayetze 154b). It says there that a certain voice is aroused from the Shechinah every day in the Garden of Eden, crying out powerfully and saying: Which of you enters and goes out and takes hold of the Tree of Life, reaches its branches, grasps its roots, eats of its fruit, sweet as honey, gives life to the soul, healing to his body, guards himself from an evil fantasy — from a fantasy that betrays the Tree of Life, that defiles the river and the stream from the source of Israel, giving death to the soul and breaking to his body — he has no permanence at all. A fantasy that defiles that source of his, because that fantasy ascends and exchanges soul for soul — the Tree of Life is removed, and the Tree of Death takes hold in him, and the soul is drawn from there. Woe to him who is uprooted through that fantasy from the Tree of Life and becomes attached to the Tree of Death — he has no branches, he never sees good, he is dry, entirely without moisture, his fruit bitter as wormwood; concerning him it is said, "he shall be like a lone shrub in the desert, and shall not see when good comes..." (Jeremiah 17:6). Because a good fantasy ascends above, takes hold of the Tree of Life, grasps its branches, eats of its fruit — all holinesses and all blessings come forth from it, inheriting life for his soul and healing for his body; concerning this it is said, "and he shall be like a tree planted by the waters, and spreads out its roots by the stream, and shall not fear when heat comes..." (Jeremiah 17:8). All matters of the world follow after thought and fantasy, and therefore "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" — because all holinesses in the world come forth and are drawn through a good fantasy — so far his words. And the conclusion of this passage: therefore in prayer, will and fantasy are required to direct one's intention, and so in all the services of the Holy One, blessed be He, fantasy and thought accomplish the deed and draw down the flow of whatever is needed — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:28: This passage clearly explains our intent — whether regarding the holiness of thought, that what it says, "and you shall sanctify yourselves," and so on, refers to the holiness of thought; and likewise regarding an evil fantasy that uproots itself from the Tree of Life, which is in Atzilut. And there are two aspects to such a fantasy, as explained in the passage: first, a mere fantasy that leads to impurity, as they said, of blessed memory, that one should not fantasize by day and come to impurity by night; this is what it says, "guard yourself from an evil fantasy, from a fantasy that betrays the Tree of Life, defiling the river and the stream from the source of Israel" — this is the blemish to the sign of the Covenant (ot brit), which is called "river," "stream," "source of Israel," for it is the source of the flow of the souls of Israel; and the emission of that drop, which should have brought forth a holy soul, is instead released in vain through Lilith, as explained above, and this is a great blemish to the sign of the Covenant. The second: fantasizing about another woman during marital relations, called "children of substitution" (bnei temurah), as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Nedarim 20b, Tur Orach Chaim, siman 240).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:29: Now, from what it says, "because a good fantasy ascends above, takes hold of the Tree of Life...," "all matters of the world follow after thought and fantasy," we may draw a third division: that every evil fantasy to commit a transgression causes a blemish, in the same way that the fantasy of performing a mitzvah brings a rectification for the soul, as they said, that a good fantasy in every detail of a mitzvah ascends above, takes hold of the Tree of Life, and so on; so too, in the reverse, it takes hold of the Tree of Death. This is what was explained above, in the first interpretation, that the author of this passage says, "he defiles himself in this world" — the intent being the defilement of thought in all matters of this world, and therefore they defile him for the World to Come, because he has been uprooted from holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:30: Regarding those of this class — may the Merciful One save us from them — it says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayikra 25a) that they are the harmful spirits of the world; after speaking of the greatness of one who acquires nefesh, ruach, and neshamah, it says, of blessed memory: fortunate is the portion of one who inherits this supernal inheritance; woe to those wicked ones whose souls do not merit in this world, all the more so in the World to Come; concerning them it is written, "and the soul of your enemies, He shall sling out, as from the hollow of a sling" (I Samuel 25:29) — for they go and roam the world and find no place to attach themselves, and become defiled within the side of impurity, and a herald calls out and says, "if a soul commits a trespass against the Lord... [and lies]... the sanctuary of the Lord [being] defiled" (Leviticus 5:15, adapted) — for it does not enter into holiness and is not included therein, and they are the harmful spirits of the world, because they attach themselves to them [the wicked] and become defiled — so far his words. This passage makes clear, in ample detail, how they defile him for the World to Come — that they are called "the harmful spirits of the world."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:31: And in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot 70a) they raised a question about this, where Rabbi Yehudah says there that the souls of the wicked are the harmful spirits, and Rabbi Yosei said: if so, it would be good for the wicked to become harmful spirits in the world — where then is the punishment of Gehinnom, where is the evil appointed for them in that world? Rabbi Chiya said, so we have learned, and we have already established the matter: the souls of the wicked, at the hour they leave the world, several wardens of the law are appointed to receive them, to bring them into Gehinnom, and they bring them in for three judgments each day of Gehinnom; afterward they are paired with them, and they go and roam the world, and lead the wicked astray, those who have shut out repentance before them; afterward they return to Gehinnom and are defiled there — and so every day. Afterward, after going and roaming the world with them, they return to their graves, and there the worm of the body gnaws at the flesh, and they mourn over it — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:32: And likewise it is explained at the end of the passage we quoted from Parashat Vayera (99a), at the end of chapter 4, where it says: just as a person is drawn from this world, so too they draw him when he departs from this world — if toward holiness, and so on; if toward impurity, that side draws him toward itself, and he becomes as one of them, attached to them, and they are called "harmers of humanity," and so on — this being what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Zohar Parashat Acharei Mot 70a, see Parashat Mishpatim 118a), that the souls of the wicked are themselves the harmful spirits. And in our days we have seen this matter several times here in Safed, in the Upper Galilee, and there are several eyewitnesses to the matter.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:33: Therefore fortunate is he who sanctifies his soul and body in this world, so that his soul may attach itself to the supernal holy ones, to behold the pleasantness of the Lord and to visit His sanctuary. And with this, this chapter is concluded.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 5:34: Now that we have explained the general principles of holiness, we shall proceed to explain the particular forms of holiness appropriate to each and every limb, according to what is found in the words of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, and in the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:1: Since we were occupied in the preceding chapter with the matter of the holiness of thought, and that it is the essential thing in divine service for a person to attach himself to his Maker and draw holiness upon himself — as in the statement of Rashbi, peace be upon him, that we quoted, that all forms of holiness are drawn through a good fantasy — and in this same manner is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 13a), that "commandments require intention (kavanah)," and so most halachic authorities ruled — it follows that if one performed a commandment or studied Torah without intention, it is as though he had done nothing, and he must go back and do it [again]. Several Mishnayot prove this (Berachot 2:1): if one was reading in the Torah [the passage of Shema] and the time for reciting Shema arrived, if he directed his heart [to fulfilling the mitzvah], he has fulfilled his obligation. And likewise regarding his prayer: the early pious ones would tarry an hour, so that they might direct their hearts to the Omnipresent (Berachot 5:1). And likewise, one who immersed [in a mikveh] without [proper] intent for the immersion, it is as though he had not immersed (Chagigah 2:6). Further, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (see Berachot 34b, Tur Orach Chaim, siman 101), that if one did not direct his intention in the [blessing of the] Patriarchs [in the Amidah], he must go back to the beginning, and so on. All these are settled halachot, showing that a person's rectification of his thought is through intention (kavanah). Therefore we saw fit to explain in this chapter the way a person sanctifies his thoughts and the fantasies of his heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:2: The vessels of thought, as is known, are two: the brain and the heart, and upon them depend love and awe, as we quoted the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the Gate of Love, chapter 2, that concerning these it is said, "the hidden things belong to the Lord our God" (Deuteronomy 29:28), and as he likewise explained in the Zohar (Parashat Naso 123b): "the hidden things" are awe and love, which are in the brain and the heart, within the cavity of the body and in the head; and "the revealed things" are Torah and the commandments, which are in the body and the head, on the outside. And the mystery of the matter is truly so: if a person fears the Holy One, blessed be He, or loves Him, another person certainly does not know this, for it is a matter revealed only between him and his Maker; but a person who occupies himself with Torah and walks in the positive commandments is revealed to every person, because the Holy One, blessed be He, made for him a mouth openly, to occupy himself with Torah, and eyes to look and ears to hear it, and the Holy One, blessed be He, made for a person hands and feet to perform the positive commandments with them — so far his words. And he explained there, just before this, that love and awe are Yod-Heh, and concerning them "the hidden things belong to YHVH our God" — which are Abba and Imma; "the revealed things" are Vav-Heh, which are the Son and the Daughter, Torah and the commandment, and they are revealed because they are seen by people through the visible limbs, as explained in the passage.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:3: And so it is also in the reality of the matter in the supernal Atzilut, as is explained in the Introduction to the Tikkunim (17a), in the words of Elijah, of blessed memory: he says that the reality of the visible limbs is: Chesed, the right arm; Gevurah, the left arm; Tiferet, the torso; Netzach and Hod, the two legs; and Yesod, the end of the body, the sign of the holy Covenant; Malchut, the mouth — we call it the Oral Torah; the brain, Chochmah — it is thought within; Binah, the heart, and through it the heart understands. Concerning these two it is written, "the hidden things belong to YHVH our God" — so far his words. Thus the visible limbs are from the six extremities downward, which is "Vav-Heh, revealed," and the brain and heart, which are hidden within the body, are Chochmah and Binah, and they are hidden for two reasons: first, in the physical reality of the limbs themselves, being within the cavity of the body; and second, because the brain is the vessel in which thought rests, and thought is spiritual and hidden, and the heart is the vessel in which understanding rests, for a person to understand and know — which is also a hidden action. This is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, was precise about in saying, "the brain is Chochmah, it is thought within," and "so Binah is the heart, and through it the heart understands" — to indicate the two aspects mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:4: And in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 247b) it explains that the three "brains" in a person — meaning the three faculties within the brain — correspond to the three Yods in the Name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei (spelled out), in these words: further, "mixed with beaten oil" (Numbers 28:5) — this is the Righteous One, life of the worlds, who draws forth holy drops that are crushed like olives from the supernal brain, one-tenth [an issaron] corresponding to Yod (10), two-tenths corresponding to Yod-Yod (20), and three-tenths — these are the one-tenth for the lamb, two-tenths for the ram, and three-tenths for the bull. And the mystery of the matter is stated in [the tractate on] fasts (25b): no drop descends without two rising to meet it — and these are in the mystery, corresponding to three brains: one, the brain of memory; the second, the brain of thought; the third, the brain of imagination. Imagination and memory ascend from the heart; thoughts descend upon them to the heart and are received by them as by a king, because this is the thought that rides and rules over the third living creature, and two living creatures descend to it, opening their wings to receive it, like a cholam over a tzeirei forming a special combination — and this is the supernal Keter over Chochmah and Binah — so far his words. And likewise in the Tikkunim (126a) they explain the three brains corresponding to the three Yods of the Name mentioned — see there. We are forced to say that these three brains are in Ze'ir Anpin, for in Arich [Anpin] there is one hidden brain, as is explained in the Idra.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:5: Now, once a person knows that his whole body and its limbs were built according to the order of the supernal Atzilut, as is explained in the Tikkunim (130b), whose wording we quoted in the Gate of Awe (ch. 9), and knows that his thought corresponds to the supernal Thought, he should direct his intention so that the limbs of his brain and heart — the most esteemed limbs, upon which the vitality depends — be made ready to intend and think holy thoughts, and he should purify his thoughts as is fitting. For if he thinks improper thoughts in his brain and heart, the power of Chochmah and Binah withdraws from him. The reason is that just as the visible limbs become blemished through physical transgression, so these primary hidden limbs become blemished through impure thought; and once it is blemished, the supernal King does not cause His spiritual power of Chochmah and Binah to rest there. And this is likewise proven in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz 196a) regarding Joseph the Righteous, peace be upon him, that he was rewarded for every limb that he did not blemish, and it says regarding thought, in these words: a thought that he did not think is called "understanding and wise" — so far his words. Therefore the rectification of the brain and heart is to think holy thoughts, and by this one causes the Name Yud-Kei-Vav-Kei to rest in the thought of his brain and heart, and he should intend toward the source of holiness, which is the fully-spelled-out four-letter Name with the Yods, which numerically equals 72 (Ayin-Bet) — and by this he sanctifies his thoughts.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 6:6: By this the words of Rashbi, peace be upon him, quoted in the previous chapter, are precise, where he says, "and therefore, 'and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy,' because all holinesses in the world come forth and are drawn through a good fantasy." And you already know what we explained above in chapter 2, that Chochmah is the source of holiness, in the mystery of the Name mentioned, since there is no holiness [quorum] with fewer than ten; and fortunate is he who intends this while occupied with Torah, to draw the kindness of the aforementioned Name upon his thought — for he will certainly sanctify himself, since the Torah draws down holiness, as is explained in Parashat Kedoshim, that the Torah is drawn from Chochmah; and by directing his intention toward the source of holiness he certainly draws down holiness. In these words (Zohar 81a): We have learned, the holiness of the Torah is a holiness that surpasses all holinesses, and the holiness of the supernal Chochmah surpasses everything. He said to him, there is no Torah without Chochmah, and no Chochmah without Torah, and so on — so far his words, as pertains to our subject.
